Topology

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Geometry and topology
OurBigBook.com Words: 33k Articles: 538
Topology studies topological spaces through open sets and continuous maps. Its central equivalence is a homeomorphism: a bijection that preserves continuity in both directions. This lets us distinguish spaces by connectedness or compactness even when numerical metric values are irrelevant. The open interval (0,1) and the real line have the same topology in this sense, although only the former is a bounded set with its usual metric.
The upper panels show an explicit homeomorphism and the inverse image test for a continuous map. The lower panels exhibit an obstruction to a homeomorphism: removing any point from a circle leaves a connected space, whereas removing an interior point from a closed interval gives two connected components.
Homotopy is a different notion: it varies a continuous map continuously with a parameter and may collapse points. For example, H(x,t)=(1−t)x contracts [0,1] to zero. Thus this closed interval and a singleton have the same homotopy type, but there is no homeomorphism between them because there is no bijection. Homotopy equivalence need not preserve compactness. [ref]
The abstract viewpoint already appears explicitly in Tietze's 1923 paper: he describes topology as the study of properties invariant under invertible continuous maps with continuous inverses, and discusses axioms for neighbourhoods, citing Hausdorff's 1914 book, page 213. [ref]

On the real plane, take the initial topology of all separately continuous real-valued functions. Rectangular bump functions show that no sequence from the nonzero rational grid converges to the origin, so the space is not first countable either.

Fix a point a of an uncountable set X and declare F closed when a∈F or F is countable. Finite unions and arbitrary intersections satisfy the closed-set axioms. Every convergent sequence is eventually constant: the countable set of its values different from the limit is closed, so its complement is a neighborhood of the limit. A space is zero-dimensional when its topology has a base of clopen sets. In the Hausdorff setting these sets separate distinct points, so the space is totally disconnected. Conversely a compact Hausdorff totally disconnected space has a clopen base, by the Šura-Bura component lemma and finite subcovers of the complement of a neighborhood.

In a normal Hausdorff space, strong zero-dimensionality means that any disjoint closed sets can be separated by a clopen set, equivalently by disjoint clopen neighborhoods. For general Tychonoff spaces, the usual definition asks this for completely separated sets. In the normal setting Urysohn's lemma makes the formulations agree. Conversely separate the traces of the low and high level sets of a continuous f:βX→[0,1] by clopen U⊆X. The characteristic function of U extends into {0,1} on βX. Density ensures its one level contains the zero level of f and misses the one level. Applying this with f separating a point from a closed set gives a clopen base for βX.

A Hausdorff compactification is a compact Hausdorff space K with a topological embedding j:X→K whose image is dense. It retains the original topology on X while adjoining boundary points. For a locally compact noncompact Hausdorff space, its one-point compactification is an example. For every Tychonoff space, the Stone-Čech compactification extends all continuous maps into compact Hausdorff targets.

If a locally compact Hausdorff space is densely embedded in a Hausdorff space, its image is open. Around a point choose an ambient open set whose trace lies in a compact neighborhood K. Density puts that ambient open set inside the ambient closure of its trace, which lies in K because compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed. Thus the ambient open set lies in the image.

For a Hausdorff compactification h:R→Y, let C± be the intersections of the closures of the positive and negative tails, respectively. Each is nonempty and connected by the closed-filter-base theorem. Their union equals the remainder: an image point has a bounded-interval neighbourhood excluding sufficiently long tails, whereas every neighbourhood of a remainder point meets tails by density and compactness of bounded intervals. If the remainder is finite, each C± must be a singleton, so there can be only one or two remainder points. In particular there is no three-point compactification of the real line.

The compact Baire category theorem makes ⋂n​(Gn​∩On​)=⋂n​Un​ dense in K, hence in X. Therefore every Čech-complete space is a Baire space. The rationals are not a Baire space, as deleting their points one at a time gives dense open sets with empty intersection.

For two topologies on the same set X, σ is finer than τ when every τ-open set is σ-open. Equivalently, the identity function (X,σ)→(X,τ) is continuous, by the definition using preimages of open sets. The inclusion may be an equality; strictly finer means proper inclusion.

The topological disjoint union of topological spaces Xi​ has the labelled disjoint union as its underlying set. A subset is open exactly when its intersection with each labelled copy Xi​ is open in that copy. Each copy is a clopen set, and a function from the topological disjoint union is continuous exactly when its restriction to every copy is continuous. This follows immediately by testing preimages of open sets on each copy. A topological space is homeomorphic to the topological disjoint union of its connected components exactly when all those connected components are open.

Topology OurBigBook.com
A topological invariant is a property or mathematical object preserved by homeomorphisms of topological spaces. Connectedness and compactness are examples. The fundamental group is an invariant up to group isomorphism; it is also preserved up to isomorphism by homotopy equivalence, a stronger invariance property which does not hold for every topological invariant.

Topology OurBigBook.com
An end of a noncompact topological space describes a coherent way to escape every compact subset. For a cofinal compact exhaustion, when one exists, K1​⊆K2​⊆⋯, it is represented by nested connected components of the complements. A connected noncompact manifold is disconnected at infinity when it has more than one end.

Orientability

Words: 342
Topology OurBigBook.com
Orientability asks whether local choices of handedness can agree everywhere on a manifold. On a smooth manifold, an orientation of a smooth manifold chooses an orientation of a vector space for each tangent space, continuously with position. An ordered basis describes the same handedness as another one when the change-of-basis determinant is positive. An oriented atlas implements this condition through positive Jacobian determinants of the smooth transition maps.
A paper strip makes the obstruction visible. Join its short ends without twisting: the resulting untwisted band admits a consistent choice of unit normal. Add a half-turn before joining: on the Möbius band, following the core circle of a Möbius band reverses that choice when you first return to the same point. A local decision about handedness has encountered a global contradiction. The normal reversal around the Möbius core makes this precise for an explicit model.
Both rectangles have coordinates (u,v)∈[0,1]×[−1,1]. The untwisted band identifies (0,v) with (1,v); the Möbius band identifies (0,v) with (1,−v). Across a seam the corresponding local coordinate changes preserve or reverse v, giving determinants +1 and −1. This sign explains the handedness change; the drawing also tracks the two boundary circles of the untwisted band and the single boundary circle of the Möbius band.
For a smooth topological surface embedded in R3, choosing an orientation of a surface is equivalent to choosing a continuous unit normal. This picture is specific to surfaces in three-dimensional space: the general definition uses compatible local orientations, without requiring an embedding. Orientability is a topological invariant, so a homeomorphism cannot turn a Möbius band into a untwisted band. The sphere and torus are orientable surfaces; the Klein bottle is not. [ref]
The distinction matters when a sign has geometric meaning. A signed flux surface integral needs an orientation of a surface, and Stokes theorem relates that choice to the outward-normal-first boundary orientation. Ordinary unsigned surface area does not require orientability. Thus a Möbius band still has a perfectly meaningful area even though it has no continuous global unit normal.
A connected orientable manifold of positive dimension has two possible orientations: reversing every local choice gives the other one. If a manifold has several connected components, each component can be oriented independently when it is orientable. For topological surfaces, a useful obstruction criterion is the presence of a Möbius band: a surface is nonorientable exactly when it contains such a band. [ref]

A non-Hausdorff manifold is a locally Euclidean topological space for which distinct points need not have disjoint neighborhoods. The real line with two origins is a basic example. Nonseparated algebraic schemes exhibit analogous gluing phenomena, but are not generally topological manifolds.

Take R×{0,1} with its Euclidean topology and identify (t,0) with (t,1) for every t=0, retaining two distinct origins. This quotient space is locally homeomorphic to the real line but is not Hausdorff. Any open neighbourhoods of its origins have preimages containing (−ε,ε)×{0} and (−δ,δ)×{1}, so a nonzero ∣t∣<min(ε,δ) gives a shared image point. All equivalence classes in the original metric space are finite and closed. This shows that closed equivalence classes do not suffice for a Hausdorff quotient space.

Topology OurBigBook.com
A Stone space is a compact Hausdorff space that is totally disconnected, equivalently a compact Hausdorff space with a basis of clopen sets. The topology on a type space gives an important example.

The nonempty open sets are the upper tails of the natural numbers. Arbitrary nonempty unions select the smallest starting index, and finite intersections select the largest, so these sets form a topology. A map into this space is continuous exactly when the inverse image of every upper tail is open.

For a map f:N→N from the cofinite topology to the tail topology on the natural numbers, continuity is equivalent to every set {n:f(n)≥k} being empty or cofinite. If the image is unbounded, every such set is nonempty and cofinite, so f(n)→∞. If it is bounded, its maximum M exists, and the inverse image of the tail at M forces f(n)=M eventually, with f(n)≤M always. Conversely either condition makes every tail preimage empty or cofinite.

Topology OurBigBook.com
The Fell topology on the closed subsets of a locally compact space has subbasic open sets requiring intersection with an open set or avoidance of a compact set. On a locally compact separable metric space, its sequential convergence says that every convergent subsequence of points from the varying sets has its limit in the limiting set, and every point of the limiting set is approximated by points from the varying sets.

These sets form a topology: a nonempty union of upper rays is another upper ray, or all of R when their endpoints have no lower bound; a finite intersection of rays has endpoint the maximum of their endpoints. The whole line must be included. The continuous map n↦n from N with the cofinite topology to this space is nonconstant, because each upper ray has cofinite inverse image.

For the topology consisting of the empty set, the whole real line, and upper open rays, a nonempty subset is compact exactly when it has a smallest element. An open set containing the smallest element contains the entire subset. Conversely, if there is no smallest element, the rays (a,∞) indexed by points a of the subset cover it, but any finite selection misses its smallest chosen endpoint.

Topology OurBigBook.com
A topological space is hyperconnected if any two nonempty open sets intersect. Every continuous map from a nonempty hyperconnected space to a Hausdorff space is constant: two distinct image points would have disjoint open neighbourhoods whose nonempty inverse images contradict hyperconnectedness. Every infinite set with the cofinite topology is hyperconnected.

Topology OurBigBook.com
A closed cover of a topological space is a family of closed sets whose union is the whole space. A finite closed cover can be used in separation and antipodal arguments: in a metric space, vanishing distance to a closed member means actual membership. Unlike an open cover, a closed cover does not automatically have a partition of unity subordinate to its members.

Topology OurBigBook.com
Given a partition of a set, declare a subset open precisely when it is a union of partition blocks. Arbitrary unions and finite intersections of such unions are again unions of blocks, giving a topology. The quotient map to the block set with its discrete topology pulls that topology back to the original set. For the partition of Z into its two parity classes, the only open sets are the empty set, those two classes, and all of Z.

Topology OurBigBook.com
On an infinite set, the family consisting of all finite subsets and the whole set need not be closed under arbitrary unions. On Z, the union of the singleton subsets of 2Z is infinite and proper, so this family is not a topology. It must not be confused with the cofinite topology, whose proper open sets have finite complements.

The lower limit topology on R has basis of a topology {[a,b):a<b}. Every such nonempty interval contains a rational, so this topological space is separable. Its topology is finer than the usual Euclidean topology; the one-sided basic neighbourhoods allow its square to have an uncountable discrete antidiagonal.

The Sorgenfrey plane is the product topology on two copies of the Sorgenfrey line. It is separable because Q2 meets every nonempty basic rectangle [a,b)×[c,d). Its antidiagonal {(x,−x):x∈R} is an uncountable discrete subspace: [x,x+ϵ)×[−x,−x+ϵ) meets it only at (x,−x). In a discrete space every dense subset is the whole space, so this subspace is not separable. Thus separability need not pass to subspaces of nonmetrizable spaces.

A topological space is extremally disconnected when the closure of every open set is open. This concerns open sets, not arbitrary subsets. In particular, a nonisolated singleton in a Hausdorff space is closed but not open, so its closure gives a counterexample to that stronger condition.

The open sets are the empty set and subsets whose complement is countable. On an uncountable set, any two nonempty open sets intersect, so the space is not Hausdorff. On a countable underlying set this topology is discrete. The compact subsets of a cocountable space are finite, regardless of the cardinality of the underlying set.

Only finite subsets are compact in the cocountable topology. An infinite subset contains distinct c1​,c2​,…. The open sets obtained by removing the tails {cj​:j≥n} form an increasing open cover, but every finite selection misses a tail point. Finite sets are compact in every topology.

A family (Ai​) of subsets of a topological space is locally finite if every point has a neighbourhood meeting only finitely many of its members. On a compact space such a family has only finitely many nonempty members. For singleton subsets of a Riemann surface, this is the condition permitting prescribed poles of a meromorphic function without accumulation inside the surface.

Topology OurBigBook.com
The indiscrete topology on a set X has only the empty set and the whole set as open sets. When X has more than one point it is not a Hausdorff space. For example the quotient topology on R/Q is indiscrete: a nonempty open saturated subset contains an interval and all its rational translates, which cover R.

A triangulation of a surface decomposes it into triangles meeting along full edges or vertices. On a closed surface, each edge is incident with two triangle faces, so 3F=2E. Euler characteristic connects this local counting relation with the surface's topology.

Topology OurBigBook.com
If a topological space is the union of finitely many closed subspaces and continuous maps on those subspaces agree on every overlap, they combine into a continuous map on the whole space. For a closed set in the target, its preimage is a finite union of closed sets, proving continuity.

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Topology OurBigBook.com
The cofinite topology on a set X declares the empty set and all cofinite subsets to be open sets: a nonempty open set may exclude only a finite set of points. There is no assumed metric. On an infinite set, this gives a particularly small collection of open sets while still making every singleton a closed set. On a finite set, every subset has finite complement, so the cofinite topology is the discrete topology.[ref]
For an original example, use X=N>0​ and choose
U=X∖{2,5,8},V=X∖{1,3,7}.
(1)
Both are open sets, and their intersection is U∩V=X∖{1,2,3,5,7,8}. Thus 4,6,9,10,… are in both. Their finite exclusions cannot separate the infinite remainder. The finite intersection of any finite collection of nonempty open sets is again a nonempty open set, since its complement is a finite union of finite sets. An arbitrary nonempty union is open because its complement is contained in the finite complement of any one nonempty member.
The cofinite topology is useful for separating hypotheses that familiar metric spaces package together. An infinite cofinite topological space is a T1 space, because its singletons are closed, but is not a Hausdorff space, because two nonempty open sets cannot be disjoint sets. It is a hyperconnected space and hence a connected space. Moreover, every subset of a cofinite space is compact, and sequence convergence in the cofinite topology can have many limits. These are compatible properties, rather than contradictions: the usual uniqueness and closedness results use the Hausdorff space hypothesis.[ref]

Let Z be the underlying set of real numbers with the cofinite topology. The diagonal W={(t,t):t∈R} in Z×R with its subspace topology is homeomorphic to the usual real line. Indeed, t↦(t,t) is a continuous bijection: its first coordinate is continuous because usual finite sets are closed, and its second coordinate is the identity. The inverse is the second coordinate projection restricted to W. Consequently W is not compact, whereas Z is compact by the fact that every subset of a cofinite space is compact. Thus W is not homeomorphic to Z.

Cofinite topology OurBigBook.com
For a set X with its cofinite topology, a subset S is a connected subset exactly when S is empty, a singleton, or infinite. Indeed, its subspace topology is the cofinite topology on S: the traces of open sets are precisely S∖F for finite F⊆S, together with the empty set. For infinite S, two nonempty open sets intersect, because their complements have finite union. Hence S is a hyperconnected space and therefore a connected space. A finite S has the discrete topology, which admits a separation of a topological space as soon as S has at least two points.

For an infinite set X with its cofinite topology, every infinite subset is connected, but X×X has an infinite disconnected topological subspace. Choose a=b and use D={a,b}×X. The open sets (X∖{b})×X and (X∖{a})×X have disjoint nonempty traces {a}×X and {b}×X on D, covering it. Thus D is a product of a discrete two-point subspace with an infinite cofinite factor. The ambient open rectangles may intersect; only their traces must be disjoint for a separation of D.

By convergence of a sequence in a topological space, xn​→a means that every open neighbourhood of a contains all sufficiently late terms. In the cofinite topology, this is equivalent to the condition that, for every b=a, the value b occurs only finitely often. Necessity uses the open neighbourhood X∖{b}; sufficiency chooses an index beyond every last occurrence of the finitely many points excluded by a given open neighbourhood.
Consequently a sequence with distinct terms converges to every point of X. For the original choice xn​=n on X=N>0​, take the two open neighbourhoods
U1​=X∖{2,5,8}∋1,U2​=X∖{1,3,7}∋2.
(2)
All terms with n≥9 lie in U1​ and all terms with n≥8 lie in U2​. More generally, each finite excluded set has a last visit, so xn​→1 and xn​→2, and in fact xn​→a for every a∈X. No numerical distance is tending to zero here; the open sets specify the meaning of convergence.
Distinct terms are sufficient, not necessary. The sequence 1,1,2,2,3,3,… also converges to every point, since each value occurs only twice. By contrast, the constant sequence xn​=1 converges only to 1: an open neighbourhood of any a=1 can exclude 1. The alternating sequence 1,2,1,2,… converges to no point, since some value different from any proposed limit occurs infinitely often.

On X=N>0​, the subset of even integers is compact but not closed, because it is infinite and proper. A compact subset of a Hausdorff space is guaranteed to be closed, whereas compactness without the Hausdorff space assumption does not suffice. Changing the topology changes compactness: the same infinite set with its discrete topology has the singleton open cover, which has no finite subcover. Otherwise two distinct image points would have disjoint open neighbourhoods. Their inverse images would be nonempty disjoint open sets of X, contradicting its hyperconnected space property.
For example, f(n)=n from N>0​ with its cofinite topology into the real line with its usual Euclidean metric is not continuous: the inverse image of the open interval (1/2,3/2) is {1}, which is not open in the infinite domain. Closed set (X∖F∈τ)

Words: 547 Articles: 4
Topology OurBigBook.com
A subset F of a topological space (X,τ) is closed when its complement in that same ambient space is open: X∖F∈τ. For example, the closed interval [0,1] is closed in the usual real line because its complement is the open set (−∞,0)∪(1,∞). Always specify the ambient topological space: a subset can be closed in a subspace topology without being closed in the surrounding space. [ref]
Being closed is not the logical negation of being open. In the usual real line, all four combinations occur: (0,1) is open but not closed; [0,1] is closed but not open; the half-open interval [0,1) is neither open nor closed; and both the empty set and the whole real line are open and closed, hence clopen. Nor does being closed imply being a bounded set: [0,∞) is closed because its complement (−∞,0) is open, but it is not a bounded set. The symbol ∞ is not an extra point that this interval must contain.
The coloured strokes mark membership; filled endpoint circles mean included points, and hollow endpoint circles mean excluded points. The empty set has no coloured points, while arrows at both ends of the coloured real line indicate that membership continues indefinitely. These examples use the usual topology of the real line.
In a metric space X, a subset F is closed exactly when every convergent sequence (xn​) in F whose limit of a sequence x lies in X has x∈F. For example, xn​=1−1/n lies in [0,1) for n≥1 and has limit of a sequence 1, which is missing; thus this half-open interval is not closed in the real line. This criterion is useful for keeping limiting constructions inside a prescribed set. [ref]

A sequentially closed set is one that contains every limit of its convergent sequences. This is weaker than being a closed set in a general topological space, but the two conditions agree in metric spaces.

A subset of the plane can have three successive strict changes under taking its set of accumulation points. For example let
A={(n1​+n2m1​,n2m2k1​):n,m,k≥1}.
(3)
Put B={(1/n+1/(n2m),0):n,m≥1} and C={(1/n,0):n≥1}. Then A′=B∪C∪{0}, A′′=C∪{0} and A′′′={0}, where 0 denotes the origin. For fixed n,m, increasing k gives a point of B; increasing m gives a point of C; increasing n gives the origin. These are all possible limits: in any convergent sequence of distinct points, either n is unbounded, or a subsequence fixes n and has unbounded m, or a subsequence fixes both and has unbounded k. The first-coordinate cluster intervals [1/n,1/n+1/n2] are disjoint and separated away from the origin. Repeating this classification after each differentiation proves the displayed derived sets. The closure of a subset A of a topological space X is the smallest closed set containing A. Equivalently, it is the intersection of all closed sets containing A, or the set of points whose every neighbourhood in X meets A. The notation clX​A makes the ambient topological space explicit. This definition works without a metric or any appeal to sequences. [ref]
For A=[0,1) in the usual real line, A=[0,1]: every neighbourhood of 1 meets A, while a point outside [0,1] has an open ball disjoint from A. Passing to the closure adds the missing endpoint and retains all original points, including isolated points when present. In general, the closure is A together with its limit points; its individual points are the adherent points of A.
The closure turns an arbitrary subset into a closed set with no unnecessary added points. It satisfies A⊆A and A=A; a subset is closed exactly when A=A. In a metric space, x∈A exactly when some sequence of points of A has limit of a sequence x: choose its nth point in A∩B(x,1/n). For a general topological space, keep the neighbourhood definition; sequences need not detect every point of the closure.

A point lies in A∘=intX​A exactly when it has an open neighbourhood contained in A. In a metric space, this says that some open ball B(x,r), with r>0, is contained in A. The interior therefore identifies the points with room to move locally while staying in A. [ref]
For the half-open interval A=[0,1) in the real line, A∘=(0,1). Every point strictly between the endpoints has a sufficiently small open ball inside A, but every open ball about zero also contains negative points. Although 0∈A, it is not in the interior; it is a boundary point instead. Together, the interior and closure bracket the original subset: A∘⊆A⊆A.

They describe different topological spaces on the same set: the first is Hausdorff and disconnected, while the second is connected and not Hausdorff. Each is compact because X is a finite set.
The identity function i:(X,τd​)→(X,τi​) is a continuous map: the only target open sets have inverse images ∅ and X. A Lindelöf space is a topological space in which every open cover has a countable subcover. A closed discrete subset of a Lindelöf space must be countable: cover each of its points by an open set meeting it at only that point and add the open complement. In a metrizable space, the Lindelöf property is equivalent to topological separability.

Topological space OurBigBook.com
Choose an uncountable set X and a point a∈X. Every point other than a is isolated, and a set containing a is open precisely when its complement is countable. Equivalently, the closed sets are all subsets containing a together with all countable subsets. Arbitrary intersections and finite unions preserve this latter condition, so it defines a topology.
Every convergent sequence in this space is eventually equal to its limit. Indeed the set of its values different from its limit is countable and closed; its complement is an open neighbourhood of the limit. Eventual membership in this complement forces eventual equality. Nevertheless a is not isolated, because its singleton has uncountable complement. In particular sequence convergence alone does not determine this topology.
A real-valued function on this space is continuous exactly when {x:f(x)=f(a)} is countable. Sufficiency follows by considering the preimages of closed subsets of the real line: each either contains a or is a subset of that countable exceptional set. For necessity, each set {x:∣f(x)−f(a)∣≥1/n} is closed and excludes a, hence is countable; their countable union is the exceptional set.

Topological space OurBigBook.com
A topological space is first-countable when each point has a countable neighbourhood basis. Every metric space is first-countable: the open balls B(x,1/n) form such a basis. A subset of a first-countable space remains first-countable in its subspace topology, since intersecting a local basis with the subset preserves the defining containment property. Thus a space failing first countability cannot be homeomorphic to any subset of a metric space.

Topological space OurBigBook.com
The Warsaw circle joins the two path components of a closed topologist's sine curve by an arc attached at their outer endpoints. It is path-connected and has trivial fundamental group, yet admits a continuous map to the circle with no continuous lift to its real-line covering space. Set the map equal to 1 on the closed topologist's sine curve and wind once on the joining arc. A lift would be constant on each path component of the sine curve, with the same constant on both by continuity, but would change by 1 along the joining arc. This proves that the map is not null-homotopic, by the homotopy lifting theorem for a covering map. Thus finiteness of the fundamental group alone cannot replace local path connectedness in the usual lifting criterion for a covering space.

An open map sends each open set to an open set; a closed map sends each closed set to a closed set. These properties concern images, whereas continuity concerns inverse images of open sets. Neither openness nor closedness alone implies continuity.

A topological space is regular when a point and a closed set not containing it have disjoint open neighborhoods. Equivalently, for every point x in an open set U, there is an open W with x∈W⊆W⊆U. q:X⟶X/∼,q(x)=[x].
(14)
The quotient topology is defined by the rule using preimages of open sets:
τq​={U⊆X/∼:q−1(U)∈τX​}.
(15)
Thus a subset of the quotient space is open if and only if its entire preimage is open in X. Each fiber q−1({[x]}) is the whole equivalence class [x], so the preimage includes every point glued to any of its members.[ref]
This is the finest topology making q a continuous map: every topology with that property can contain only subsets whose preimages are open. It really is a topology, because preimages preserve the empty set, the whole set, arbitrary unions, and finite intersections. The gluing example below shows why checking a complete preimage matters, especially at the seam.
The quotient topology also makes continuous maps out of a glued space easy to construct. A continuous map f:X→Z descends to a unique continuous map fˉ​:X/∼→Z exactly when it is constant on every fiber of q, meaning x∼y⇒f(x)=f(y). Define fˉ​([x])=f(x); the equivalence class representative cannot affect the answer. For every open set V⊆Z,

For the canonical projection of a quotient set p:X→X/∼, the saturation of A⊆X is the union of all equivalence classes meeting A, namely p−1(p(A)). A subset is called saturated when it equals its saturation. The quotient topology says that p(A) is closed exactly when the saturation of A is closed, and similarly for openness. A closed set need not have closed saturation: collapsing (0,1)⊂R to one point makes the saturation of {1/2} equal to (0,1). Hence a quotient map need not be a closed map.

Quotient topological space (X/∼)

Words: 605 Articles: 2
Quotient topology OurBigBook.com
A quotient topological space is a quotient set equipped with the quotient topology. For a concrete gluing, give the closed interval I=[0,1] its usual subspace topology, identify 0∼1, and leave every interior point in its own singleton equivalence class. The resulting quotient space is a circle: the two endpoints become one point, while interior points remain distinct.
The exact continuous map to the unit circle in the plane is
p(t)=(cos(2πt),sin(2πt)),pˉ​([t])=p(t).
(18)
Here sine and cosine give p(0)=p(1)=(1,0), and p(s)=p(t) holds exactly when s=t or {s,t}={0,1}. Thus p induces a bijection pˉ​:I/∼→S1. [ref] The universal property of the quotient topology makes pˉ​ continuous. The quotient of a compact space is compact, and the unit circle is Hausdorff, so the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem makes pˉ​ a homeomorphism. This verifies the topology, not merely the point identifications.
To inspect an open neighbourhood of the seam, choose 0<ε<1/2 and let Uε​=p([0,ε)∪(1−ε,1]). Its full preimage is
p−1(Uε​)=[0,ε)∪(1−ε,1].
(19)
Both pieces are open in the subspace topology on I, so Uε​ is open in the circle. In contrast, A=[0,ε) is open in I, but
p−1(p(A))=[0,ε)∪{1}
(20)
is not open in I: it contains 1 without any neighbourhood of 1. Hence p(A) is not open in the circle. A quotient map can therefore fail to be an open map.
For a continuous function f:I→R, the only gluing condition is f(0)=f(1). For example, f(t)=cos(2πt) defines a continuous function on the circle, whereas f(t)=t does not. This lets us use an interval as a coordinate for a periodic function while making the seam invisible. More general quotient spaces encode glued geometric pieces in the same way: describe continuous maps before gluing and check that their values agree on every equivalence class.
The Hausdorff property need not survive a quotient topology. In the non-Hausdorff quotient of the real line by rational translation, x∼y means x−y∈Q. A nonempty open preimage W must contain all translates by rational numbers of any open interval inside it. The density of the rational numbers then forces W=R: for any y, some rational number r has y−r in that interval. Thus this quotient space has the indiscrete topology. The irrationality of the square root of two gives distinct equivalence classes for 0 and 2​, so this quotient space is not Hausdorff. Unlike the endpoint-gluing circle, this gluing identifies a dense subset with each point.

Sphere with its equator collapsed (S2/S1≅S2∨S2)

Words: 120
Quotient topological space OurBigBook.com
Collapse the equator of a sphere S2 to a single equivalence class and leave every other point in its own class. The two closed hemispheres are disks sharing that equator. A disk with its boundary collapsed is a sphere, so the two hemisphere quotients are spheres sharing just one point: their wedge sum. An explicit map sends height t∈[0,1] and longitude θ on the upper hemisphere to (1−cosπt,sinπtcosθ,sinπtsinθ), and sends the lower hemisphere to the sphere centred at (−1,0,0) by reversing the first coordinate. The equator goes to the common origin and the poles go to (±2,0,0). This map is continuous and has precisely the collapsed equator as its only nonsingleton fibre. Its induced map is a homeomorphism by the compact-to-Hausdorff continuous bijection theorem.

Compact Hausdorff quotient by a closed equivalence relation

Words: 144
Quotient topological space OurBigBook.com
Let X be a compact Hausdorff space and R⊆X×X a closed equivalence relation. The quotient space X/R is compact and Hausdorff. Indeed, the saturation R[C] of any closed C⊆X is the projection of the compact set R∩(C×X), so is closed. Thus the quotient map is a closed map.
Two different equivalence classes are disjoint compact subsets of X and have disjoint open neighbourhoods U,V. To see the latter assertion, separate each pair of points by disjoint neighbourhoods and use compactness twice to extract finite covers. Now U′=X∖R[X∖U] and V′=X∖R[X∖V] are open saturated subsets containing the respective classes, and lie inside U,V. Their quotient images are disjoint open neighbourhoods, proving the Hausdorff condition. Compactness follows from the continuous quotient map. This applies to finite gluing along closed boundary pieces when the generated equivalence relation is closed; that last condition must be checked.

To prove the assertion, let W⊆B×[0,1] have open preimage O, and take (b,t)∈W. Choose e∈q−1(b) and a compact neighbourhood K of t with {e}×K⊆O. The set EK​={u:{u}×K⊆O} is open by compactness of K, and is saturated under q because membership in O depends only on q(u) and the second coordinate. Hence q(EK​) is open by the quotient topology. The rectangle q(EK​)×intK is a neighbourhood of (b,t) contained in W, proving that W is open. This justifies parameterized homotopies defined on quotient spaces.

An open set is a member of the topology on a topological space. In a metric space, a subset U is an open set precisely when every x∈U has an open ball B(x,r) contained in U for some r>0. For U=(0,1), one can take r=21​min(x,1−x). At x=0.2, this gives r=0.1 and B(x,r)=(0.1,0.3)⊂U. The radius depends on the point; no uniform radius is required. [ref]

Similarly, the whole closed interval A is both an open set and a closed set in itself. These relative open sets are what the continuity test uses for maps involving a subset with its subspace topology.
Arbitrary intersections of open sets need not be open sets: ⋂n≥1​(−1/n,1/n)={0}, a singleton that is not an open set in the usual real line. Any point x=0 is excluded once n>1/∣x∣. This is why the topology axiom specifies finite intersections.

Enumerate all intervals with rational endpoints, using the countability of the rational numbers and listing pairs of enumeration indices by increasing sum. Distinct points cannot have the same index, so this gives an injective function into N and proves that B is a countable set. Compact space

A topological space X is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover: whenever open sets Ui​ satisfy X=⋃i∈I​Ui​, some finite selection satisfies X=Ui1​​∪⋯∪Uim​​. A subset K of an ambient topological space is compact when its subspace topology is compact; equivalently, every open cover of K by ambient open sets has a finite subcover. The word every matters: finding one finite subcover of one open cover is not enough to establish compactness. [ref]
The closed interval [0,1] is compact by the Heine-Borel theorem. For a concrete open cover, take the three open intervals (−0.1,0.45), (0.35,0.8), and (0.7,1.1). Their union is (−0.1,1.1), so they cover every point of [0,1], including both endpoints. The overlaps have lengths 0.1 and 0.1, leaving no gaps. Each member is necessary for this particular open cover: removing them respectively leaves 0, 0.5, or 1 uncovered.
Above, hollow markers denote the excluded endpoints of the covering open intervals, while the solid endpoints belong to the covered closed interval. Below, each displayed open interval is one member of an infinite open cover of (0,1); finitely many rows always leave points near zero uncovered. The rows are vertically separated for readability and all refer to the same real line.
The open interval (0,1) is a bounded set but is not compact: the open sets
Un​=(1/n,1),n≥2,
(26)
give an open cover of (0,1), since every 0<x<1 has 1/n<x for sufficiently large n. These are also open sets for the subspace topology on (0,1). Any nonempty finite selection has a largest index N, so its union is just (1/N,1) and misses the point 1/(N+1), which still belongs to (0,1). Thus no finite subcover exists, however many members we select. The same family is not an open cover of [0,1], since it misses both endpoints.
In a metric space, compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness: every sequence in the subset has a convergent subsequence whose limit of a sequence belongs to that subset. This equivalence does not extend to all topological spaces. For example, xn​=1/n for n≥2 has limit of a sequence zero in [0,1]. The same sequence lies in (0,1), but every subsequence still has limit of a sequence zero on the real line, so no subsequence converges to a point of (0,1). Merely approaching a boundary is harmless when the required point remains available. [ref]
Both panels show the sequence xn​=1/n for n≥2 approaching zero. In the closed interval, zero is an allowed limit of a sequence; in the open interval, the hollow marker identifies the missing point. This single sequence disproves sequential compactness of (0,1); compactness of [0,1] still requires control of every open cover or every sequence, supplied by the Heine-Borel theorem.
An infinite set with the discrete topology similarly fails compactness, using the open cover by all its singletons. Every finite set is compact in any topology: select one covering open set for each point. The empty set is compact because the empty selection is a finite subcover. This open cover definition does not require the topological space to be Hausdorff; in algebraic geometry it is often called quasi-compactness.
The beauty of compactness is that information valid around each point can often be controlled using finitely many regions. A finite subcover lets us combine finitely many local bounds, or choose the smallest of finitely many positive tolerances, to obtain control across the whole compact space. This is why compactness repeatedly turns approximation into existence and why it is so useful in optimization through the extreme value theorem.
Every closed set in a compact space is compact, and a continuous image of a compact space is compact. The latter proof pulls an open cover back by inverse images, selects a finite subcover, and maps forward. This makes compactness useful for proving existence: the extreme value theorem guarantees that a continuous function from a nonempty compact space to the real line attains both a minimum and a maximum. For example, q(x)=x(1−x)=1/4−(x−1/2)2 on [0,1] has maximum 1/4 at 1/2 and minimum zero at its endpoints. On (0,1) its infimum is still zero but is never attained. [ref]

Since compactness depends only on the topology, choosing a different norm does not change the conclusion. Without an appropriate topology, a bare vector space alone has no notion of compactness.

In the l2 sequence space, an infinite-dimensional vector space that is also a Hilbert space, let en​ be the vectors of its standard orthonormal basis. All lie in the closed unit ball B={x:∥x∥≤1}, which is a closed set and a bounded set in the norm topology. For distinct indices, their inner product is zero, giving
∥en​−em​∥2=∥en​∥2+∥em​∥2−2Re⟨en​,em​⟩=2.

For a sequence in a bounded set, apply the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem to each of the Cartesian coordinates in turn, retaining a subsequence at each of the finitely many steps. The final subsequence is a convergent sequence in all Cartesian coordinates, and a closed set contains its limit of a sequence. This yields sequential compactness, hence compactness. An involute is the curve traced by the end of a taut string as it is unwound from a fixed curve. For a circle of radius R, one parametrization is x(θ)=R(cosθ+θsinθ,sinθ−θcosθ). The straight free length is Rθ, and differentiation shows that the traced velocity is perpendicular to the taut string. Reversing the motion winds the string back around the circle.
Winding time around a circular pole (thit​=L2/(2Rv))
Words: 117
Involute OurBigBook.com
A point mass attached to a light inextensible string winds around a fixed smooth circular pole of radius R. Let the initial straight free length be L, and assume the string remains taut without slipping over the part already laid on the pole. Since its tension is perpendicular to the point mass's velocity, the speed v stays constant. If the contact point turns through dθ, the free length s obeys ds=−Rdθ, while the involute geometry gives v=sθ˙. Thus ss˙=−Rv, or s2=L2−2Rvt. First contact of the point mass with the pole occurs at s=0, after L2/(2Rv). In the ideal model, the required tension mv2/s diverges at contact; finite string strength or finite particle size limits that idealization.

Lemniscate of Bernoulli ((x2+y2)2=a2(x2−y2))

Words: 45
Plane curve OurBigBook.com
A figure-eight plane curve with two congruent lobes and a crossing at the origin. With scale a>0, its polar equation is r2=a2cos2θ. One quarter has coordinates x=at(1+t2)/2​, y=at(1−t2)/2​, 0≤t≤1. Differentiation gives arc element adt/1−t4​. The total arc length is therefore 4a∫01​dt/1−t4​.

Astroid (∣x/a∣2/3+∣y/a∣2/3=1)

Words: 40
Plane curve OurBigBook.com
An astroid is the four-cusped plane curve parametrized by x=acos3t, y=asin3t for a>0. It appears as the relative trajectory in the astroid motion of a harmonic oscillator in a rotating frame. The parametrization has zero first derivative at the cusps while remaining smooth as a function of its parameter.

Plane cusp of type (2,5) (x2−y5=0)

Words: 93 Articles: 1
Plane curve OurBigBook.com
This irreducible plane branch has parametrization x=t5, y=t2. Its only singular point is the origin. The resolution of the (2,5) cusp by two blowups makes its strict transform smooth in every characteristic.
Resolution of the (2,5) cusp by two blowups ((x,y)=(t5,t2)⟼(u,y)=(t3,t2)⟼(v,y)=(t,t2))
Words: 69
Plane cusp of type (2,5) OurBigBook.com
Blow up the origin and use the chart x=uy, giving the strict transform u2−y3=0. Blow up its remaining singular point and use u=vy, giving v2−y=0, which is smooth because its derivative in y is −1. The complementary chart at each stage has no point of the strict transform on its exceptional divisor. These two blowups of a smooth algebraic surface resolve the branch, although the smooth transform is still tangent to an exceptional divisor.

Archimedean spiral (r=a+bθ)

Words: 87 Articles: 1
Plane curve OurBigBook.com
An Archimedean spiral has radius linear in polar angle, r=a+bθ. For the special parametrization (ucosu,usinu), the curvature of a plane curve is (u2+2)/(1+u2)3/2. Its parameter speed is 1+u2​, so it remains a regular curve at the origin.
Scaled length of an Archimedean spiral (lima→0+​aLa​=R2/2)
Words: 51
Archimedean spiral OurBigBook.com
Let an Archimedean spiral have polar radius r=at and angle t in polar coordinates, with 0≤t≤R/a, where R>0 is fixed. Parameterizing by r gives the arc length
aLa​=∫0R​a2+r2​dr.
(34)
The bounds r≤a2+r2​≤r+a yield
2R2​≤aLa​≤2R2​+aR.
(35)
The squeeze theorem proves the displayed limit. Thus the arc length grows like R2/(2a) as the turns become closely spaced, without requiring an explicit antiderivative.

Superelliptic curve

Words: 51
Plane curve OurBigBook.com
A superelliptic curve has an affine equation ym=f(x). When f is square-free and the characteristic does not divide m, projection to the x-coordinate is a finite morphism whose finite ramification occurs over the roots of f; its behavior at infinity depends on m and degf.

Canonical map of a smooth plane curve

Words: 29
Plane curve OurBigBook.com
For a smooth plane curve of degree d≥4, adjunction gives
KC​≅OC​(d−3).
(36)
Its canonical map is induced by the (d−3)rd Veronese map and is therefore an embedding.

Semicubical parabola (y2=x3)

Words: 56 Articles: 1
Plane curve OurBigBook.com
A semicubical parabola is a cusped cubic curve affinely equivalent to y2=x3.
Coordinate ring and singularity of the semicubical parabola
Words: 43
Semicubical parabola OurBigBook.com
The homomorphism
k[x,y]→k[t],x↦t2,y↦t3
(37)
has kernel (y2−x3) and image k[t2,t3]. The quotient is therefore an integral domain, so the curve is irreducible. In characteristic zero its gradient (−3x2,2y) vanishes at the origin, making the origin its unique singular point of an algebraic variety.

Euler spiral

Words: 65
Curve OurBigBook.com
The Euler spiral is the planar curve parametrized by the Fresnel integrals. In the optical convention,
C(u)+iS(u)=∫0u​eiπt2/2dt.
(38)
The tangent has unit length and argument πu2/2, so its signed curvature is πu, proportional to signed arc length. In Fresnel diffraction, an interval integral is the directed chord joining its endpoint parameters on the Cornu spiral. Chord length gives the interval factor's modulus, while chord direction gives its complex argument.

Closed curve

Words: 20
Curve OurBigBook.com
A curve γ:[0,1]→X whose endpoints agree, γ(0)=γ(1). This is the same unbased notion as a loop; self-intersections are allowed.

Asymptote

Words: 51
Curve OurBigBook.com
An asymptote of an unbounded curve is a straight line whose distance from the curve tends to zero along a specified end. For a graph, a sloping asymptote y=mx+b satisfies y(x)−(mx+b)→0 as x tends to the relevant infinity. Factorization of the leading quadratic part locates the two asymptotes of a nondegenerate hyperbola.

Parametric curve (Q(t))

Words: 325 Articles: 6
Curve OurBigBook.com
A parametric curve is described by a vector-valued map t↦Q(t). Its derivative gives a tangent vector wherever it is nonzero.
// Target: geometry-and-topology.bigb

Lissajous curve

Words: 25
Parametric curve OurBigBook.com
A Lissajous curve is a parametric curve with coordinates x(t)=Asin(at+δ) and y(t)=Bsin(bt). The frequency ratio and phase shift control its crossings and whether its trajectory closes.

Parametric plane curve

Words: 23
Parametric curve OurBigBook.com
A parametric curve in the plane, given by two coordinate functions x(t),y(t). Its speed is x′(t)2+y′(t)2​ wherever these derivatives exist, giving its arc length by integration.

Parametric curve interrogation

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Parametric curve OurBigBook.com
A parametric curve interface supplies its parameter domain, evaluation, and derivatives where they exist. Robust geometric algorithms also need restricted subcurves and certified range or derivative bounds on parameter intervals. Tangent, speed and curvature are derived from point and derivative enquiries when the relevant derivatives are regular. Finite point samples alone cannot certify the absence of every plane intersection of an arbitrary smooth curve.
Certified curve-plane intersection (F(t)=n⋅C(t)−d)
Words: 91
Parametric curve interrogation OurBigBook.com
Intersecting a parametric curve with a plane reduces to isolating zeros of a scalar function. A certified range for F rejects intervals that do not contain zero. On an interval whose derivative range excludes zero, a sign-changing endpoint bracket gives exactly one root, which bisection method or a safeguarded Newton root-finding iteration refines. Other intervals are subdivided conservatively; tangencies and coplanar pieces need multiplicity or identity tests supported by the representation. An unresolved small interval is a possible contact, not a proof of an intersection. With finitely many transverse intersections and convergent enclosures, isolation terminates to any prescribed tolerance.

Cycloid (x=R(θ−sinθ), y=R(1−cosθ))

Words: 109 Articles: 1
Parametric curve OurBigBook.com
A cycloid is the plane curve traced by a point on a circle rolling without slipping along a straight line. A parametrization with rolling radius R is x=R(θ−sinθ), y=R(1−cosθ); reversing the sign of y reflects the curve. Its cusps occur at integer multiples of 2π. A descending cycloidal arc solves the classical brachistochrone problem.
Area and length of a cycloid arch (A=3πa2,L=8a)
Words: 55
Cycloid OurBigBook.com
For the cycloid x=a(t−sint), y=a(1−cost), a>0, 0≤t≤2π, the area between the arch and its baseline is
A=∫ydx=a2∫02π​(1−cost)2dt=3πa2.
(39)
Its arc length is
L=∫02π​x′(t)2+y′(t)2​dt=2a∫02π​sin(t/2)dt=8a.
(40)
The positive sign of sin(t/2) inside this parameter interval removes the absolute value in the speed. Omitting the two endpoint cusps does not change either integral.

Space curve

Words: 141 Articles: 3
Curve OurBigBook.com
A space curve is a curve in three-dimensional Euclidean space.

Helix

Words: 133 Articles: 2
Space curve OurBigBook.com
A helix is a space curve that winds around an axis while advancing along it at a constant rate. A circular helix can be parametrized by (Rcost,Rsint,at).
Logarithmic conical helix (x(s)=(2s​coslogs,2s​sinlogs,s/2​))
Words: 67
Helix OurBigBook.com
The displayed space curve, s>0, lies on a cone and is parametrized by arc length. It has a constant tangent angle with its axis, while the turn spacing shrinks geometrically toward the limiting apex. Its curvature is 1/(2​s): differentiate its unit tangent with respect to s. Infinitely many turns accumulate at the apex with finite arc length; the apex itself is not a regular point of the curve.
Pitch of a helix (P=2πdz/dϕ)
Words: 38
Helix OurBigBook.com
The pitch is the axial displacement per complete turn. For a circular helix with z=aϕ+b, the signed pitch for increasing angle is 2πa, and its magnitude is 2π∣a∣. Pitch is independent of the cylinder radius.

Inflection point

Words: 110 Articles: 1
Curve OurBigBook.com
An inflection point of a smooth plane curve is a point where its signed curvature changes sign. At a regular inflection point the curvature vanishes.

Stationary inflection point (f′(a)=0)

Words: 85
Inflection point OurBigBook.com
An inflection point of the graph of a differentiable real function at which its derivative is zero. It has a horizontal tangent and a change of concavity, but need not be a local maximum or minimum. For a three-times continuously differentiable function, f′(a)=f′′(a)=0 and f′′′(a)=0 suffice: the expansion f′′(a+h)=f′′′(a)h+o(h) gives opposite signs on the two sides. The elementary example is f(x)=x3 at zero. The word “saddle” is sometimes used for this one-dimensional situation in elementary examination papers, but the usual saddle point of a scalar function has a multivariable meaning; do not merge the two concepts.

Logarithmic spiral

Words: 65 Articles: 1
Curve OurBigBook.com
A logarithmic spiral has polar equation r=Aebθ. Its tangent meets each radial line at a constant angle.

Logarithmic spiral as an embedded real line (h(t)=et(cost,sint))

Words: 47
Logarithmic spiral OurBigBook.com
The map h is a homeomorphism from the real line to its image with the subspace topology: its continuous inverse is h−1(x,y)=logx2+y2​. Different parameters have different radii, so winding does not destroy injectivity. The origin is an accumulation point of the spiral but is not a point of this space.

Simple curve

Words: 20
Curve OurBigBook.com
A simple curve is an injective curve, apart from the permitted coincidence of its two endpoints when it is closed.

Space-filling curve

Words: 19
Curve OurBigBook.com
A space-filling curve is a surjective continuous map from an interval onto a region of dimension at least two.

Topology OurBigBook.com

Knaster-Kuratowski-Mazurkiewicz lemma

Words: 110 Articles: 3
Topology OurBigBook.com
For a simplex with vertices indexed by 0,…,n, let closed sets Fi​ have the property that every face spanned by an index set I lies in ⋃i∈I​Fi​. Then ⋂i=0n​Fi​ is nonempty. The triangle KKM lemma is a two-dimensional covering formulation of this simplex-intersection principle.

Triangle KKM lemma

Words: 66 Articles: 2
Knaster-Kuratowski-Mazurkiewicz lemma OurBigBook.com
If three closed sets cover a triangle and respectively contain its three opposite sides, then their triple intersection is nonempty.

Distance-function barycentric map

Words: 26
Triangle KKM lemma OurBigBook.com
Normalized distances to three closed sets give continuous barycentric coordinates; a covering forces at least one coordinate to vanish, placing the image on the simplex boundary.

No-retraction covering principle

Words: 20
Triangle KKM lemma OurBigBook.com
A closed-cover intersection statement for a simplex is equivalent to the nonexistence of a boundary-valued map that preserves every face.
